prompt.context: Our client is the CEO of Fancy Truck, a producer of trucks that sells mostly to logistics services companies. Fancy Truck's main current product is a truck called Evolution. Now they came up with a new engine, and they want to start selling another type of truck, called Revolution, that will use this engine. The only difference between Revolution and Evolution is the engine and Fancy Truck's plan is to have both Evolution and Revolution in the market.
prompt.question: The CEO hired us to help him find out a pricing strategy for Revolution. How would you approach this?

clarifying_info.q: Who are the main competitors and do they have a similar product?
clarifying_info.a: Nobody has a similar model — there are no direct competitors for the Revolution engine.

clarifying_info.q: What does the Evolution sell for?
What are the key differences between Evolution and Revolution?
clarifying_info.a: The only difference is the engine. Revolution can do 25% more kilometers with the same fuel. Both trucks have a 4-year useful life and the same salvage value.

clarifying_info.q: How much do customers drive per year?
clarifying_info.a: On average, clients drive 250 thousand km per year.

clarifying_info.q: What is the price of fuel?
Are there incremental costs to produce Revolution?
clarifying_info.a: Fixed costs are the same for both, but Revolution costs Fancy Truck $10,000 more to produce each unit due to the more complex engine.

exhibits.title: Market Survey — Revolution Demand at Different Price Points
exhibits.shows: A table showing three candidate prices for Revolution and the estimated percentage of customers who would buy Revolution versus Evolution at each price point.

framework: Understand customer needs: identify what logistics company drivers, purchasers, and maintenance teams care about when choosing between models
Pricing strategy selection: consider competitor-based, cost-based, and value-based approaches; with no comparable competitor product, value-based pricing is paramount
Quantify the value delivered to the customer: calculate fuel cost savings over the truck's useful life to determine maximum willingness to pay
Analyze demand at each price point using market survey data to determine profit-maximizing price
Consider behavioral/market adoption risks: why might some customers still buy Evolution even if Revolution delivers more value?
Synthesize into a recommendation for the CEO

questions.prompt: What do you think customers' main considerations are when comparing Evolution and Revolution — what matters when deciding which one to buy?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use a clear structure such as Driver Needs (fuel efficiency, comfort, reliability), Purchaser/Fleet Manager Needs (total cost of ownership, price, financing), and Maintenance Needs (parts availability, repair complexity, mechanic familiarity). Key answers: price, fuel efficiency, durability, maintenance costs, parts availability, driver familiarity.

questions.prompt: How would you come up with a price for the new Revolution truck?
questions.guidance: Candidate should mention three approaches: (1) Competitor-based pricing — not applicable here since no competitor has a similar model. (2) Cost-based pricing — cost plus markup. (3) Value-based pricing — determine how much extra value Revolution delivers to customers and price accordingly. Interviewer should push candidate toward value-based since that is the most relevant method here.

questions.prompt: Given the specifications below, how much do you think we could charge for Revolution? Evolution sells for $100K; Revolution gets 25% more km per liter; both have a 4-year useful life; clients drive 250K km/year; fuel is $1.50/L; Evolution fuel efficiency is 10 km/L.
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute the 4-year fuel cost for each truck, find the savings that Revolution provides, and add that to Evolution's price to get the maximum willingness to pay. A strong answer explicitly sets up the NPV/savings calculation and arrives at $130K as the ceiling price.

math.setup: Calculate 4-year total fuel cost for Evolution and Revolution, then find the difference (= value of Revolution's fuel savings to customer). Add this to Evolution's price ($100K) to get maximum price for Revolution.
steps: Evolution fuel consumption per year: 250,000 km / 10 km/L = 25,000 L/year
Evolution fuel cost per year: 25,000 L * $1.50/L = $37,500/year
Evolution total fuel cost over 4 years: 4 * $37,500 = $150,000
Revolution fuel consumption per year: 250,000 km / 12.5 km/L = 20,000 L/year
Revolution fuel cost per year: 20,000 L * $1.50/L = $30,000/year
Revolution total fuel cost over 4 years: 4 * $30,000 = $120,000
Fuel savings from Revolution over 4 years: $150,000 - $120,000 = $30,000
math.answer: Maximum willingness to pay for Revolution is $130,000

questions.prompt: Fancy Truck conducted a market survey (see Exhibit 1). Fixed costs are the same for both trucks, but Revolution costs $10K more per unit to produce. Which of the three prices — $100K, $115K, or $130K — would you recommend for Revolution, and why?
questions.guidance: Candidate must ask for cost information before concluding (goal is profit maximization, not revenue maximization). Key insight: at $100K, Revolution yields zero price premium over Evolution but costs $10K more to make — so it is strictly worse to sell Revolution at $100K. Compare incremental profit per 100 trucks at $115K vs $130K. $130K dominates. Candidate should note that market size is not needed to reach this conclusion — the ratio of incremental profit per unit sold is sufficient.

math.setup: For each price, compute incremental profit per Revolution unit (price premium over Evolution minus extra unit cost of $10K) multiplied by the number of Revolution units sold (as % of total). Compare across price points.
steps: At $100K: price premium over Evolution = $0; extra cost = $10K; incremental profit per unit = $0 - $10K = -$10K. Selling Revolution at $100K destroys value — eliminate this option.

At $115K: price premium = $115K - $100K = $15K; extra unit cost = $10K; incremental profit per Revolution unit = $15K - $10K = $5K; % buying Revolution = 80%; per 100 trucks: 80 Revolution units * $5K = $400K incremental profit

At $130K: price premium = $130K - $100K = $30K; extra unit cost = $10K; incremental profit per Revolution unit = $30K - $10K = $20K; % buying Revolution = 40%; per 100 trucks: 40 Revolution units * $20K = $800K incremental profit
math.answer: Price Revolution at $130K; incremental profit per 100 trucks is $800K vs $400K at $115K

brainstorming.prompt: Why do you think some people would still buy the old Evolution model even if the price of Revolution was the same?

categories.name: Risk & Uncertainty
ideas: Logistics companies do not want to replace their entire fleet before testing the new truck and confirming the fuel efficiency claims
Customers may be uncertain whether real-world performance will match the stated 25% efficiency gain

categories.name: Maintenance & Parts Availability
ideas: No old Revolution engines exist in the market, so third-party repair and replacement parts could be harder to find
Customers may fear it will be difficult to find mechanics experienced with the new engine
Downtime risk is higher for a new, unproven engine type

categories.name: Organizational & Operational Inertia
ideas: Fleet managers may have existing service contracts tied to Evolution
Drivers and maintenance staff are already trained on Evolution; retraining takes time and money
Procurement processes may favor known, approved suppliers/models

recommendation: Price Revolution at $130,000 — this is both the value-based ceiling (equal to Evolution's price plus $30K in 4-year fuel savings) and the profit-maximizing price given the demand survey ($800K incremental profit per 100 trucks vs $400K at $115K)
Maintain Evolution in the product line at $100K to serve customers not yet ready to adopt Revolution, capturing the full market
risks: Actual fuel savings may differ from the 25% claim if customers' driving patterns deviate from the 250K km/year average, reducing willingness to pay
New engine may face higher-than-expected maintenance costs or reliability issues, damaging brand reputation
At 40% adoption, a significant portion of customers prefer Evolution — slow adoption may delay payback on Revolution R&D
next_steps: Conduct a pilot with a subset of logistics clients to validate the 25% fuel efficiency claim under real operating conditions
Develop a financing or TCO (total cost of ownership) calculator to help fleet purchasers visualize the $30K lifetime savings
Build out the mechanic training and spare parts supply chain to reduce customers' maintenance risk concerns before broad launch
